title: Neighbour joining as a named distance algorithm
dek: Wikipedia NJ: a fast agglomerative tree from a distance matrix. Not a likelihood, not automatically consistent under the wrong distance.
story: Neighbour joining on Wikipedia is an algorithm: start from pairwise distances, iteratively join neighbours to minimise a balanced length criterion. It is fast and used as a first look or as a starting tree for likelihood search.
It is not Felsenstein pruning. If the distance is Hamming on a recombining alignment, NJ will still return a tree — confidently wrong in geometry.
stats-trees owns the likelihood. This card names the algorithm so a methods line 'we built an NJ tree' is not dressed as a model.
deep: Additive distances (tree-like) make NJ consistent; long-branch attraction still exists in other methods.
UPGMA assumes a clock; NJ does not. That is why NJ replaced UPGMA in many TB snapshots.
Bootstrap of NJ is a bootstrap of a distance algorithm, not of a likelihood.
Do not report NJ branch lengths as years.
